To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed an adenovirus-based reporter vector for the detection of CTCs and demonstrated the feasibility of this approach in an animal model of breast cancer.
the adenovirus‐mediated reporter vector is a novel method for detecting viable and specific CTCs.
the use of an adenovirus reporter vector to infect circulating tumor cells (CTC) allows for their identification and isolation in a highly sensitive and specific manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an adenovirus vector that can specifically detect viable CTCs.
the development and validation of a novel approach for the isolation of viable and tissue‐type specific CTCs.
developing a novel adenoviral vector for the detection of viable CTCs and the identification of tissue‐specific CTCs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the detection of CTCs in the blood of cancer patients is a very useful tool in cancer diagnosis, prognosis, prediction of response to treatment, and in the follow‐up of patients.
the use of the Ad‐CMV‐GFP vector in the detection of viable and tissue‐speciﬁc CTCs in the blood of cancer patients is a novel and effective approach.
the use of the Ad‐Cre reporter vector for CTC detection is a novel and promising approach for the identification of rare CTCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a new adenovirus‐mediated gene delivery system to detect viable CTCs in the blood stream.
we have developed an adenovirus-based reporter vector that is capable of specifically infecting and expressing a fluorescent reporter gene in CTCs.
we have developed an adenovirus-based reporter vector that is able to identify viable and tissue-specific CTCs in the blood of cancer patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
adenovirus-based reporter vectors can be used to detect viable and tumor-specific CTCs.
the adenoviral vector‐based reporter system can be used for the specific and sensitive detection of viable CTCs.
the adenovirus‐mediated expression of the human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) reporter gene can be used for the specific detection of viable and tissue‐originated CTCs.
